description: Cross-cutting wiring and infrastructure checks: equipment zone_id propagation, FuelType enum consistency, ThermalCategory tagging, EndUse string consistency, postcard serialization stability, HaresError variant usage and SimError panic wrapper, and ND interpolation extrapolation.

reviews.title: Equipment zone_id propagation: HPXML → config → init → step → PortContribution, no zone_id=0 leakage
reviews.prompt: Every piece of equipment is associated with a thermal zone. The zone_id must propagate correctly through the full equipment lifecycle: HPXML parsing → equipment config → init() → step() → PortContribution. A broken chain anywhere results in thermal contributions attributed to the wrong zone (or to no zone at all, silently discarding the equipment's thermal output). Review the propagation chain: (a) HPXML parsing: verify that the HPXML parser extracts the correct zone reference from the equipment element and resolves it to the internal zone ID. HPXML may reference zones by ID string or by adjacency to conditioned space. (b) Config construction: the resolved zone_id must be stored in the equipment configuration struct. Verify that every equipment config struct has a zone_id field (not just HVAC equipment—water heaters, batteries, and PV inverters may also have zone associations for thermal losses). (c) Init: the init() function must accept the zone_id from config and store it in the equipment's runtime state. Verify that init() does not hardcode zone_id=0 or ignore the config's zone_id. (d) Step: step() must emit PortContribution values tagged with the correct zone_id. Verify that every PortContribution emitted by equipment carries the zone_id from its runtime state. (e) No zone_id=0 leakage: zone_id=0 typically means 'unassigned' or 'outdoor'. Indoor equipment must never emit zone_id=0 because the telemetry accumulator would route the contribution to the outdoor bucket or to a nonexistent zone. (f) Outdoor equipment: equipment that is physically outdoors (PV panels, outdoor condenser units, some battery systems) should route its PortContribution to zone_id=None or a designated outdoor zone, not to an indoor zone. Verify this distinction. (g) Multi-zone equipment: some equipment serves multiple zones (e.g., a ducted system with zone dampers). Verify how the zone_id is represented for multi-zone equipment—as a list, a primary zone with secondary zone list, or as separate per-zone contributions. (h) Zone topology changes: if the dwelling model supports adding/removing zones at runtime, verify that equipment zone references are updated atomically.

reviews.title: FuelType enum consistency: HPXML fuel strings map to correct enum, all fuel types in port accumulation
reviews.prompt: The FuelType enum maps fuel source strings to internal fuel categories. Consistency errors cause fuel consumption to be attributed to the wrong fuel type, breaking energy cost calculations and emissions estimates. Review: (a) HPXML fuel string mapping: HPXML uses specific fuel type strings: 'natural gas', 'electricity', 'propane', 'fuel oil', 'wood', 'wood pellets', 'coal', 'solar', etc. Verify that each recognized HPXML string maps to the correct FuelType variant. 'natural gas' must map to FuelType::NaturalGas, not FuelType::Gas or FuelType::Propane. A typo in the mapping string ('natural_gas' vs 'natural gas') causes the fuel to be unrecognized and defaulted. (b) Unrecognized fuel strings: what happens when an HPXML file specifies 'kerosene', 'diesel', 'anthracite coal', or 'district heating'? The parser should produce an error, not silently default to FuelType::Electricity (which would attribute fossil fuel consumption as zero-emission electric). (c) Complete enumeration: verify that every FuelType variant is used in the port accumulation and telemetry code. A FuelType variant that exists in the enum but has no accumulator bucket silently drops consumption data. (d) Dual-fuel equipment: heat pumps with electric backup, or dual-fuel systems (heat pump + gas furnace), consume two fuel types. Verify that each equipment step() can emit PortContribution values for multiple fuel types and that the accumulator sums them correctly without double-counting. (e) Electricity source subdivision: some analyses need to distinguish grid electricity from on-site solar electricity. Verify whether FuelType has separate variants for grid vs. solar electricity, or whether this distinction is handled elsewhere (e.g., through net metering in the tariff layer). (f) Unit consistency: fuel consumption in the port system should be in consistent energy units (Joules). Natural gas HPXML specifications are typically in Btu or therms; the conversion to Joules must use the correct factor (1 Btu = 1055.06 J, 1 therm = 105,506,000 J). A wrong conversion factor means all gas-related costs and emissions are off by a constant multiplier.

reviews.title: ThermalCategory tagging: HvacHeating, HvacCooling, DuctLoss, JacketLoss, InternalGain correctly set
reviews.prompt: Every thermal PortContribution must be tagged with the correct ThermalCategory so that the telemetry system can disaggregate thermal loads by source. Untagged or incorrectly tagged thermal contributions produce misleading load breakdowns. Review: (a) HvacHeating: any heat delivered to a zone by a heating system (furnace, heat pump, electric resistance, boiler) must be tagged HvacHeating. Verify that auxiliary/backup heating (heat strip, dual-fuel backup) is also tagged HvacHeating, not a separate category. (b) HvacCooling: any heat removed from a zone by a cooling system (air conditioner, heat pump in cooling mode) must be tagged HvacCooling. Verify that the sign convention is consistent: cooling is negative heat addition. (c) DuctLoss: heat lost from ducts passing through unconditioned space (attic, crawlspace, garage) must be tagged DuctLoss, not HvacHeating or HvacCooling. Verify that duct losses to conditioned space are NOT tagged DuctLoss (they're not losses to the dwelling as a whole). (d) JacketLoss: heat lost from water heater tank jackets, storage tanks, and hydronic piping in unconditioned space must be tagged JacketLoss. Verify that jacket losses to conditioned space are tagged as InternalGain (they reduce the heating load). (e) InternalGain: heat from occupants, appliances, lighting, electronics, and cooking must be tagged InternalGain. Verify that the split between sensible and latent internal gains is preserved. (f) Solar gain through windows: verify whether solar gains are tagged with a separate ThermalCategory (SolarGain) or grouped into InternalGain. Solar gains have different temporal patterns and should ideally be identifiable separately. (g) Infiltration heat gain/loss: verify whether infiltration thermal exchange is tagged separately (Infiltration) or embedded in the envelope load. Infiltration loads can be 20-40% of total heating/cooling and should be separately identifiable for retrofit analysis. (h) Untagged contributions: audit all step() methods across all equipment types and the envelope solver. Any thermal contribution that reaches PortContribution without a ThermalCategory tag should either be rejected at compile time (if the ThermalCategory is a required field) or logged as a warning at runtime. (i) Category naming consistency: verify that ThermalCategory variant names use a consistent naming convention and are documented with their expected usage.

reviews.title: EndUse string consistency: audit for typos, inconsistent naming, missing end-uses, HPXML alignment
reviews.prompt: EndUse strings label energy consumption by purpose for reporting and HPXML compliance. Inconsistent naming produces reports that disaggregate the same end-use into multiple categories or lump different end-uses together. Review: (a) Complete enumeration: list all EndUse string values defined in the codebase. Compare against the HPXML end-use categories: heating, cooling, water heating, lighting, appliances, electronics, cooking, laundry, dishwasher, pool pump, hot tub, EV charging, etc. Any HPXML end-use not represented in HARES means consumption of that type is mislabeled or unlabeled. (b) Typo audit: grep every EndUse string literal in the codebase. Common typos include 'heating' vs 'heeting', 'lighting' vs 'lightning', 'appliance' vs 'apliance'. A typo creates a new end-use category that will appear as a separate line item in reports. (c) Naming consistency: verify that the same end-use is not called 'WaterHeating' in one place and 'DHW' or 'water_heating' or 'Water Heating' elsewhere. Pick one convention (HPXML uses 'water heating') and enforce it. (d) Missing end-uses: some equipment may not tag its consumption at all (missing EndUse in PortContribution). Audit each equipment step() method for PortContribution creation and verify the EndUse field is always populated. (e) HPXML compliance: HPXML and Building America use specific end-use category names. Verify HARES EndUse strings match the expected names for interoperability with HPXML-based reporting tools (BEopt, OpenStudio, URBANopt). (f) New end-use addition: when a new equipment type is added (e.g., a pool heater), the developer must know to add a new EndUse string. Verify that the EndUse system makes it obvious where to add new values (a centralized enum or const list, not scattered string literals). (g) EndUse in metrics: verify that metrics reports aggregate by EndUse correctly—summing all contributions with the same EndUse string across all timesteps and dwellings. Case-sensitive string matching can cause 'Heating' and 'heating' to be reported as separate categories.

reviews.title: Postcard serialization stability: checkpoint format across Rust versions, field change detection
reviews.prompt: HARES uses postcard for checkpoint serialization. The checkpoint format must be stable across Rust compiler versions and the serde implementation used. Checkpoint corruption is catastrophic because it's silent—the deserialization succeeds but produces wrong values, and the simulation continues with corrupted state. Review: (a) Cross-version stability: postcard does not guarantee wire-format stability across versions. Check whether the version of postcard is pinned in Cargo.lock and whether the serialized format is documented with a format version number embedded in the checkpoint file. If postcard changes its encoding between versions, old checkpoints become unreadable or silently corrupt. (b) Field addition/removal: adding a new field to a checkpoint struct (with #[serde(default)]) is safe if the default is sensible. Removing a field is safe if the old field is ignored with #[serde(skip)] or the struct uses #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]. Verify that every checkpoint struct has a strategy for forward and backward compatibility. (c) Field type changes: changing a field from f32 to f64, from u32 to i64, or from an enum with 3 variants to 4 variants can break deserialization silently (if the serialized bits happen to deserialize to a valid but wrong value) or with an error (if they fall outside the valid range). Verify that type changes are detected in review and versioned. (d) Schema versioning: each checkpoint struct should carry a version field that is checked on deserialization. If the version doesn't match, refuse to load with a clear error message. (e) Checkpoint integrity: verify that checkpoints include a checksum (CRC32 or similar) to detect file corruption. A flipped bit in a checkpoint file should produce a checksum error, not a silently corrupted simulation. (f) Fleet checkpoint consistency: in a fleet simulation, all dwellings must checkpoint and restore at the same timestep. If dwelling-1 restores from step 1000 and dwelling-2 from step 999, the fleet is out of sync. Verify the checkpoint manager enforces per-timestep consistency across the fleet. (g) Checkpoint size: checkpoints containing large arrays (RNG state, thermal history) can be megabytes per dwelling. For a 10,000-dwelling fleet, this is tens of gigabytes. Verify the checkpoint format uses compression or sparse storage if needed. (h) Graceful failure: if a checkpoint fails to deserialize (due to format mismatch, corruption, or missing file), the simulation should produce a clear error message identifying the problem, not panic with a generic SerdeError.

reviews.title: HaresError enum variant usage: each variant returned somewhere, no catch-all Physics(...) abuse
reviews.prompt: The HaresError enum has distinct variants for different error categories: Physics, Envelope, Equipment, Io, Control, Dwelling, Tariff, InvariantViolation. Each variant should be returned from at least one code path to justify its existence, and the catch-all Physics variant should not be used as a dumping ground for unrelated errors. Review: (a) Physics: intended for physically impossible conditions (negative absolute temperature, conservation law violation, negative mass flow). Grep for Physics usage and verify every occurrence is genuinely a physics error, not a config error, IO error, or logic bug. (b) Envelope: intended for envelope model errors (singular RC matrices, invalid construction assemblies, solver non-convergence). Verify every Envelope error originates in the envelope crate. (c) Equipment: intended for equipment model errors (invalid COP, out-of-range capacity, missing performance map data). Verify every Equipment error originates in an equipment crate. (d) Io: intended for file IO, parsing, and network errors. Verify that HPXML parsing errors, URDB fetch failures, and weather file read errors use Io, not a mix of Io and Physics. (e) Control: intended for control system errors (invalid signal, priority conflict, unhandled signal type). Verify that control errors use the Control variant. (f) Dwelling: intended for dwelling-level errors (invalid dwelling configuration, missing required equipment, zone topology errors). (g) Tariff: intended for tariff errors (invalid rate structure, missing tariff data, billing calculation errors). (h) InvariantViolation: intended for post-step invariant check failures (energy not conserved, mass not conserved). This variant is special because it may trigger a panic in development mode vs. a warning in production. (i) Missing variants: are there error categories not covered by the existing variants? For example, a Network variant for HELICS communication errors? A Benchmark variant for benchmark-specific validation errors? (j) Display and Debug implementations: verify that each variant produces a useful error message that includes context (what went wrong, where, and any relevant values). A HaresError::Physics('invalid') with no details is unhelpful.

reviews.title: SimError::Panic string wrapper: panic message capture, panic hook reliability, fleet reliability impact
reviews.prompt: The SimError::Panic variant wraps a panic message as a String to capture panics that occur during simulation without crashing the entire process. In fleet simulations with thousands of dwellings, a single dwelling's panic must not bring down the entire fleet. Review: (a) Panic hook installation: verify that a custom panic hook is installed (via std::panic::set_hook) that catches the panic message and converts it to a SimError::Panic(String) rather than aborting. Check that the hook is installed before any simulation code runs and after any other hooks that might overwrite it. (b) Catch unwind: the panic must be caught with std::panic::catch_unwind at the dwelling step boundary. Verify that every step() call is wrapped, not just the top-level engine loop—a panic in a per-equipment step should be caught and scoped to that dwelling, not the engine. (c) Hook reentrancy: if the panic hook itself panics (e.g., allocating a String for the panic message when the allocator is corrupted), the process will abort despite the hook. Verify that the hook is minimal and allocation-safe. (d) Panic message capture: the default panic hook formats the panic message with file, line, and optional payload (for assert! macros). Verify that the captured String includes this context. (e) Double-panic: if catch_unwind catches a panic but the error handling code (logging, telemetry) itself panics, the process aborts. Verify that error handling code is panic-free. (f) Fleet reliability: in a fleet of 10,000 dwellings running a year-long simulation, if each dwelling has a 0.001% chance of panicking per step (131,400 steps/year), the expected number of panics is ~13,000, not zero. The fleet must survive individual dwelling panics: the failed dwelling should be marked as Failed, the remaining dwellings continue, and the fleet report includes failure statistics. (g) Panic-after-panic: if a dwelling panics in step N, is it retried in step N+1? Ideally, a failed dwelling is permanently excluded from further steps to avoid cascading failures. Verify this behavior. (h) Thread safety: in a multi-threaded fleet simulation, catch_unwind is per-thread. Verify that a panic in one thread does not poison shared state (Mutex, RwLock) used by other threads. (i) Panic message structured data: a raw panic string is hard to aggregate programmatically. Consider whether the SimError::Panic variant should additionally carry a structured error code, dwelling ID, and timestep.

reviews.title: ND interpolation extrapolation: out-of-bounds grid lookups, clamping vs. NaN strategy
reviews.prompt: Equipment performance maps (heat pump COP, battery efficiency, inverter efficiency) are stored as N-dimensional lookup tables and evaluated via interpolation. Out-of-bounds queries (extrapolation) occur when the operating point falls outside the manufacturer's data range and must be handled carefully. Review the extrapolation strategy: (a) For step() (online simulation): extrapolation should clamp to the nearest valid grid point. This is the safest strategy: a heat pump operating at -30°C when the map only goes down to -15°C should use the -15°C performance values, not extrapolate to potentially negative COP or NaN. Verify that clamping is applied per dimension, not to the multi-dimensional point (which might clamp to a corner that doesn't correspond to clamping individual coordinates). (b) For LUT generation (offline preprocessing): extrapolation should produce NaN or a sentinel value. When generating a performance map as preprocessed data for the online simulator, extrapolated values that produce NaN signal a coverage gap in the performance data that must be filled. Filling with clamped values hides the gap. (c) Extrapolation strategy selection: verify that the interpolation function accepts an enum parameter (Clamp, NaN, LinearExtrapolate, NearestNeighbor) so the caller can choose the strategy appropriate for their context. A single hardcoded strategy will be wrong for one of the two use cases. (d) Linear extrapolation dangers: linear extrapolation is mathematically simple but physically dangerous. A COP curve that is flattening (diminishing returns at higher temperatures) will be linearly extrapolated to increasing COP, overestimating performance. Conversely, a COP curve that drops steeply at low temperatures will be extrapolated to negative COP. Linear extrapolation should never be the default. (e) Multi-dimensional extrapolation: in N dimensions, a query point may be in-bounds in some dimensions and out-of-bounds in others. Verify the extrapolation handles this mixed case correctly—clamping the out-of-bounds dimensions while interpolating the in-bounds ones. (f) Grid regularity: verify that the interpolation code handles irregularly spaced grid points in each dimension. Equipment performance data from manufacturers is often irregular (more points near the typical operating range, sparse at extremes). (g) Performance: ND interpolation is called millions of times per simulation (every equipment step, every timestep). Verify the interpolation code is optimized—binary search for grid cell location (O(log N) per dimension) rather than linear scan (O(N)). (h) Cache locality: for multi-dimensional interpolation, verify the grid data is stored in a cache-friendly layout (contiguous array) with precomputed strides. (i) Off-by-one in grid search: the binary or linear search that finds the containing grid cell must handle the query point exactly on a grid point correctly (interpolation weight = 0 for the other grid vertices). A fencepost error where exactly-at-grid-point queries fall into the wrong cell produces a small but systematic error in every lookup.
